segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for problem in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El problema, good. We can see it ends in an -a, so we would expect it to be feminine, but we saw that these words ending -ma in Spanish, many of them entered through Greek, and in Greek they're neuter, but they look a bit masculine in Greek, so they came into Spanish as masculine words, even though they end in -a. So we have el problema. System?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. The paradigm, how do you think that would be in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El paradigma, good. Scheme also came in from Greek, but scheme in Spanish means outline or diagram. How do you think that would be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, and something else to make it sound a bit more Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. El esquema. We said that we cannot start s plus another consonant in Spanish. We have to put an e before, like Spain, España, spaghetti, espagueti. El esquema, so this would be outline or diagram. Diagram is another one of these words. How do you think that would be in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El diagrama, good. So mostly, words ending -o are masculine and words ending -a are feminine, but we might find some exceptions. Planeta, for example, what do you think that means, planeta?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Planeta is a masculine word, so the planet?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un planeta, very good. How would you say the planets?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Los planetas, good. So this is a masculine word that looks feminine. How was the word for car? We saw various words.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Auto. Let's let's work with that one. How do you say the car?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los autos, good. If you want to say this car, you say este auto, este auto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We saw esta noche, this night. What do you think is the difference between este and esta then, if we have este auto and esta noche, what do you think is the difference?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So we see that noche is a feminine word. How would you say the night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. But this night or tonight?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esta noche, good. If you take this t out of este and esta, the words for this, you get the word for that. So este auto is this car, and that car would be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ese auto. How would you say I want that car?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I don't want that car because it's very big. Big is grande, so how would that be in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Grande. I don't want that car because it's very big.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero ese auto porque es muy grande.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No quiero ese auto porque es muy grande. How was this night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And how would be that night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esa noche. We just get rid of the t and then we have the word for that. What if you wanted to say those nights?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esas noches, good. There are also a few words that end in -o which are feminine. For example, mano. Mano means hand, ends in -o, but it's a feminine word. So how would you say the hand?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We have this word in English like in manuscript, manual as well. Manual, manuscript, that that man bit there means hand. Maintain, which in Spanish is mantener, we have main or man means hand. Manage, manage means to handle. Actually, it has a special use for handling horses historically, which is interesting because to manage, manejar, is used in some Latin American countries to mean to drive. Other than to manage or to handle, it also means to drive, manejar. Which is interesting because this verb manage historically had a special use to handle horses, and we see how that's kind of translated over the years to driving. How would you say can you give me a hand? So this is a literal translation of something idiomatic in English, but it works in Spanish as well, in Spanish you say this. Can you give me a hand, and let's talk informally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Puedes darme or me puedes dar una mano. How would you say could you give me a hand? Could you give me a hand? So could is would can.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Me podrías dar una mano? ¿Podrías darme una mano? You should give me a hand. You should give me a hand. Should is would owe, still informal.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Deber... Debería... You should: deberías... ¿Me deberías dar una mano?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me deberías dar una mano. Here we're not asking, though, it sounded like a question.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You should give me a hand.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Give it to me again, not like a question, like an like a statement: you should give me a hand.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what if you were speaking to more than one person?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Deberían darme una mano. You guys should give us a hand.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So we said that manejar means to handle or to manage, manejar...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...and also to drive in some Latin American countries. How would you say I am managing the problem or I manage the problem?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say I'm managing the problem, and you mean right now? So I remind you that for managing, for -ar verbs, to get this -ing, we take away -ar and we put -ando, and for -er/-ir verbs, for this -ing, we take away the -er or the -ir and we put -iendo. So first part is I am managing. I am managing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy manejando el problema. So mano, we said ends in -o and it's feminine. It's actually kind of the only true word that ends in -o and is feminine. So, for example, we have la foto, the photo, but foto is short for fotografía, so it's actually la fotografía becomes la foto. The same with la moto, the motorbike is actually la motocicleta, no? But people say moto and foto and it stays with la. To take in Spanish is tomar, tomar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say I'm taking a photo, and you mean right now?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy tomando una foto. You might hear sacar as well for photo, sacar or tomar. Estoy tomando una foto, estoy sacando una foto, but let's use tomar for now. I would take a photo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tomaría una foto. I would like, so it would please me, to take a photo. So what is to please or like?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Gustar. So it would please me, I would like, it would please me to take a photo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me gustaría tomar una foto. But I don't have my camera. But I don't have my camera.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. All together: I would like to take a photo, it would please me to take a photo, but I don't have my camera.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...una foto, pero no tengo mi cámara.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Me gustaría tomar una foto, pero no tengo mi cámara. Very good.
